newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rebels say Bonn asked for kidnap case aid.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebels say Bonn asked for kidnap case aid.

text.p: Colombia's second-largest guerrilla army teamed up with a shadowy German private eye at Bonn's request in a bid to free a German kidnap victim, a rebel leader said in a communique published on Saturday.

Part of the document by Manuel Perez, a Roman Catholic priest and head of the National Liberation Army (ELN), appeared in the Bogota daily La Prensa. In it Perez said Werner Mauss, now under arrest in Colombia, had no "political or organic" links to his guerrilla organisation.

Perez rejected police allegations that the ELN and Mauss were involved in snatching Brigitte Schoene from her home in northwest Colombia in mid-August. German Embassy officials were unavailable for comment.

"The ELN denies taking part in the kidnapping of Brigitte Schoene and wishes to clarify that it acted as intermediary to secure her release at the request of the German government. It is tendentious and harmful to accuse Klauss (a name used by Mauss) and his wife in Schoene's abduction," the communique read.
"Neither Klauss nor his wife are part of this organisation. Neither do they have organic or political links with it," the document added.

The communique marked the first time the ELN has publicly commented on the arrest of Mauss near the northwest city of Medellin on Nov. 17 as he tried to bundle Schoene aboard a private charter flight out of the country.
Colombian authorities believe Mauss is the international finance chief of the ELN or, at the very least, a mercenary negotiating the release of kidnap victims in return for a cut of the ransom.
A political scandal flared when the German authorities said they were "fully informed" of Mauss' mission, which they described as a "humanitarian" rescue effort.

Shortly after Schoene's kidnapping, German diplomatic sources in Bogota said they believed she had not been abducted by the ELN, as the authorities said, but was in the hands of a right-wing paramilitary group. Paramilitary leaders contacted by Reuters denied that claim.

Five men suspected of belonging to the ELN were arrested shortly after Mauss and accused of kidnapping Schoene. The Colombian authorities, however, have a track record of blaming common criminal activities on leftist rebels.

The communique, also signed by the ELN's No. 2 leader, Nicolas Rodriguez, praised Mauss for trying to set up German-brokered peace talks with the Colombian government. The chance that such talks will be held appear to have ended with Mauss' arrest.
